summary: sed edits text line by line, most often to find and replace. awk splits each line into fields (columns) and runs a small program on them, which makes it good for reports from CSV files and logs.
notes: Without -i, sed prints the changed text and leaves the file alone. With -i it rewrites the file, and there is no undo.
In awk, {print $1, $3} runs for every line that matches the pattern before it. The comma in print adds a space.
awk does decimal math, so the average prints 82.375. Bash $(( )) would give 82.
pitfall: Using double quotes around an awk program lets bash replace $1 and $3 before awk sees them, so awk prints the wrong fields or nothing. Put awk programs in single quotes.
